catalog_quote: [Lynch 2002:866, Nukuhiva sketch after Zewen 1987] Stress is predictable, occurring on the last vowel if it is long, otherwise on the penultimate vowel: ['kopu] 'stomach' [he'nua] 'land' [u'e:] 'cry' [Mutu & Teikitutoua 2002:34-35, Ua Pou] In Marquesan two types of stress are heard, word stress and phrase stress. Word stress is predictable as is phrase stress when it is not being used for emphasis purposes. ... Within such phonological words, stress occurs on the last long vowel, or, in three-syllable words, on the first long vowel, or, if there is no long vowel, on the last diphthong, or, if there is no diphthong, on the penultimate syllable of the word. ... All single short-syllable words are, as this rule predicts, unstressed. ... Stress placement does not change before final or non-final juncture. ... [m'AtA] 'eye' [hEt'U:] 'star' [pE?'AU] 'speak' ... audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: both deciding passages (Lynch 2002:866; Mutu & Teikitutoua 2002:34-36 incl. fn.25) are verbatim in held files, and the Mutu PDF is held in full. The weakness is languoid fit, not quotation: both sources describe North Marquesan (Nukuhiva, Ua Pou) and the record extends them to South Marquesan, for which Glottolog lists no grammar or phonology at all (MEDs Kruppa 1999, Ward 1962; Ward fetched sources now and is silent on stress). The one South-specific statement I could locate and open, Charpentier & François 2015 Atlas intro pp.94-95 (Fr. 42-43), says for Hiva Oa that stress is 'generally on the penultimate', that vowel sequences are heterosyllabic ([to.to.u.a], [nu.i]) and that reduplications stress the penultimate syllable ([pa.e.ˈpa.e], [ta.u.ˈta.u]); it shows a lengthened stressed penult ([e.ka.ʔeːka]) but says nothing about final long vowels attracting stress. sources.quote: On Southern Marquesas (Hiva Oa, Tahuata, Fatu Hiva): 'the glottal stop is still heard in stressed syllables, i.e. generally on the penultimate. Thus, the word ʔekaʔeka "to be happy" is pronounced [e.ka.ʔeːka] ... still audible under stress, correlated with the lengthening of the following vowel. On the island of Hiva Oa ... all syllables are detached: totoua is pronounced in four syllables [to.to.u.a] ... When a lexeme is formed by reduplication, stress falls on the penultimate syllable: paepae [pa.e.ˈpa.e]; tautau [ta.u.ˈta.u].'
